records.subject: Algebra
records.title: Linear equations: solve 3x + 4 = 13
records.notes:

A solution to simultaneous equations must satisfy both equations at the same time. Elimination removes one variable by adding or subtracting the equations.

Worked example: x + y = 12 and x − y = 6. Adding the equations gives 2x = 18, so x = 9.

Substitute x into the first equation: 9 + y = 12. Therefore y = 3. Check the second equation: 9 − 3 = 6.

The +y and −y terms cancel when the equations are added. Keep track of signs when choosing whether to add or subtract.

records.subject: Algebra
records.title: Quadratic roots: x² − 7x + 10 = 0
records.notes:

Worked example: x² − 7x + 10 = 0. The numbers 2 and 5 add to 7 and multiply to 10, so the factors are (x − 2)(x − 5).

Set each factor equal to zero. x − 2 = 0 gives x = 2; x − 5 = 0 gives x = 5.

Expanding the factors checks the middle term and the constant. Remember that a quadratic can have two roots; finding one is not always enough.

records.subject: Algebra
records.title: Arithmetic sequences: term 11 with a difference of 3
records.notes:

records.title: Average speed: 64 km over 2 hours
records.notes:
Average speed is total distance travelled divided by total elapsed time. It measures how quickly distance accumulates and does not include a direction.

Illustrative classroom journey: a cyclist travels 64 km in 2 hours. Average speed = 64/2 = 32 km/h.

To convert km/h to m/s, divide by 3.6. This speed is approximately 8.89 m/s. Both units describe the same distance per time.

Average speed does not mean the cyclist maintained that exact speed throughout. Include stops if they are part of the total elapsed journey time.

records.subject: Physics
records.title: Newton's second law: accelerating a 22 kg trolley
records.notes:
For constant mass in an inertial frame, Newton's second law is F = ma. F is the net force, m is mass in kilograms, and a is acceleration in metres per second squared.

Illustrative classroom example: a trolley has mass 22 kg and acceleration 3 m/s². The net force is 22 × 3 = 66 N.

A newton is one kg·m/s². Substituting the values gives 66 kg·m/s², or 66 N. The net force and acceleration point in the same direction.

Use the net force after combining all forces, not just one applied force. A balanced set of forces gives zero acceleration, which does not necessarily mean zero velocity.

records.subject: Physics
records.title: Ohm's law: 22 V across a 22 Ω resistor
records.notes:
For an ohmic conductor at constant physical conditions, voltage, current, and resistance are related by V = IR. Voltage is in volts, current in amperes, and resistance in ohms.

Illustrative ideal circuit: a 22 Ω resistor has 22 V across it. Rearranging the equation gives I = V/R = 22/22 = 1 A.

Check by multiplying: 1 A × 22 Ω = 22 V. The calculation assumes the resistor's resistance remains constant.

Current flows through the resistor; voltage is measured across it. Ohm's law in this constant-resistance form is not a universal description of every electrical component.

records.subject: Physics
records.title: Density: 880 g in a volume of 110 cm³
records.notes:
Density is mass per unit volume. The formula is ρ = m/V. A density calculation must use compatible units for mass and volume.

Illustrative classroom measurement: a uniform block has mass 880 g and volume 110 cm³. Its density is 880/110 = 8 g/cm³.

Check by rearranging: mass = density × volume = 8 × 110 = 880 g. The example describes a hypothetical block rather than identifying a particular material.

Do not divide volume by mass when finding density. A larger object can have the same density as a smaller object made from the same uniform material.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.title: Moles: 240 g with molar mass 80 g/mol
records.notes:
The amount of substance in moles is n = m/M, where m is the sample mass and M is the molar mass. Using grams and grams per mole gives an answer in moles.

Illustrative classroom example: a pure sample has mass 240 g. The problem gives its molar mass as 80 g/mol; it does not identify a specific compound.

The amount is 240 ÷ 80 = 3 mol. Check: 3 mol × 80 g/mol = 240 g.

Mass and amount of substance are different quantities. Always use the correct substance's molar mass and convert kilograms to grams if M is given in g/mol.

records.subject: Computer Science
records.title: Binary conversion: decimal 36 as an unsigned byte
records.notes:
Binary is base two and uses digits zero and one. From right to left, an unsigned byte's place values are 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, and 128.

Worked example: decimal 36 is written as the eight-bit value 00100100. The positions containing a one contribute 32 + 4 = 36.

Leading zeroes keep the representation eight bits wide without changing its value. Checking int('00100100', 2) in Python also returns 36.

This is an unsigned interpretation. Signed representations have different rules for the most significant bit; do not apply unsigned place values blindly to signed data.

records.subject: Computer Science
records.title: Linear search: find 60 in an eight-item list
records.notes:
Linear search checks list items one at a time until it finds the target or reaches the end. A basic implementation starts at index zero and moves from left to right.

Worked example: search the list [30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80, 90, 100] for 60. The target is at zero-based index 3, which is position 4 when counting from one.

A left-to-right search makes 4 equality comparisons before finding this target. The number of comparisons is one more than its zero-based index.

The worst-case running time is O(n): a target at the end, or an absent target, may require checking every item. A best-case match at the first item takes one comparison.

records.subject: Computer Science
records.title: Storage units: convert 40 KiB to bytes and bits
records.notes:
One kibibyte (KiB) is 1,024 bytes. One byte is eight bits. The binary prefix KiB is different from the decimal prefix kB, which means 1,000 bytes.

Worked example: a file is exactly 40 KiB. Multiply by 1,024 to find its size: 40 × 1,024 = 40,960 bytes.

Convert bytes to bits by multiplying by eight: 40,960 × 8 = 327,680 bits. These calculations describe the logical data size, ignoring filesystem allocation overhead.

Check both the prefix and the symbol. A lowercase b commonly denotes bits; an uppercase B denotes bytes. Confusing the two introduces a factor-of-eight error.

records.subject: Economics
records.title: Simple interest: 2500 units at 5% for 1 years
records.notes:
In a simple-interest model, interest is calculated on the original principal only. The formula is I = Prt when r is the annual rate written as a decimal and t is in years.

Illustrative classroom example: P = 2500 currency units, annual rate = 5%, and time = 1 years. Interest = 2500 × 5/100 × 1 = 125 units.

The final amount in this simplified model is 2500 + 125 = 2,625 units. This hypothetical calculation excludes fees and taxes.

Simple interest differs from compound interest: it does not add previous interest to the balance used to calculate future interest.

records.subject: Economics
records.title: Break-even analysis: fixed costs of 1680 units
records.notes:
In a basic break-even model, total revenue equals total cost at the break-even quantity. Contribution per unit is selling price minus variable cost per unit.

Illustrative classroom shop: fixed costs are 1680 currency units, selling price is 40 per item, and variable cost is 28 per item. Contribution per item is 40 − 28 = 12 units.

Break-even quantity = fixed costs/contribution = 1680/12 = 140 items. Revenue is 5600; total cost is 1680 + 3920 = 5600, so they match.

This model assumes a constant selling price, constant variable cost per unit, and that every produced item is sold. It is a simplified classroom model.
